newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU finance ministers promise to press on with EMU.
newsitem.headline: EU finance ministers promise to press on with EMU.

text.p: European Union finance ministers, meeting after a turbulent fortnight that has thrown the future of the EU's single currency into doubt, on Sunday dismissed any talk of delaying the project.

Echoing comments earlier in Germany from Chancellor Helmut Kohl, ministers and other EU officials arriving for a dinner meeting said putting back the start of economic and monetary union (EMU) was not on the cards.
"No delay," European Commission President Jacques Santer said as he arrived for dinner in the EU's Kirschberg building in Luxembourg.
"It's not possible," Danish Economy Minister Marianne Jelved said, responding to a question about whether the single currency timetable would slip from its January 1, 1999 launch.
Ministers also played down the chances of a fight over the so-called stability pact, due to be would be ratified formally at a summit in Amsterdam next week, despite French concerns.
The pact, agreed in principle at a summit in Dublin in December, is designed to keep countries from running high deficits once the single currency is introduced.
French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin said during his election campaign he did not feel bound by the pact.
"We will listen to what (French Finance Minister Dominique) Strauss-Kahn has to tell us and we will see," Jean-Claude Juncker, Luxembourg's finance and prime minister, said.
He added that the pact had to suit all countries.
Finnish Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto said he was confident the pact would be ratified in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17.
The dinner was arranged for ministers to discuss the design for new euro coins.
But the evening session and the ministers' regular monthly meeting to follow on Monday have been overshadowed by turmoil in the 15-nation bloc's plans for EMU.
Sunday's talks were the first between German Finance Minister Theo Waigel and his counterparts since Bonn floated the idea of revaluing gold reserves to shore up Germany's flagging finances.
It was a move that raised questions about Germany's ability to meet the strict tests of EMU without resorting to creative accounting, something Bonn had sharply criticised others for attempting.
A compromise has been reached between Waigel and the Bundesbank, which vehemently opposed the plan, but Germany's difficulty in meeting EMU criteria has been given a clear public viewing.
Waigel said nothing as he arrived.
The ministerial meeting was also the first attended by France's Strauss-Kahn following the election triumph by Socialist-led left.
The Socialists have made clear they want an end to austerity programme their predecessors felt were necessary for France to meet the EMU criteria.
Strauss-Kahn said only that discussion of the French Socialist government's views would have wait until Monday.
"You'll see tomorrow," he told reporters.
The uncertainty has left financial and political analysts predicting that EMU will either be delayed from its January 1, 1999 start or will begin with a weaker currency in a broad range of countries.
